_note: The questions any liver-safety package must answer, independent of compound. This file is the reason the inventory is not hard-coded per drug: it lists QUESTIONS, never expected answers, so it applies unchanged to a novel chemical entity that appears in no database. Versioned and hashable for the same reason the ruleset is - an inventory that reported 'nothing missing' is only meaningful if the list it was checked against is pinned.
_whyTwoHalves: Spec section 3.4. The defect measured on 2026-08-09 was that mechanism evidence alone was allowed to produce 'do not advance'. Five of the engine's seven commitments were real bile-transport inhibitors that are approved and prescribed. Splitting the checklist is what makes 'mechanism present, consequence not established' a statable position rather than a missing vocabulary.

items.whatItBlocks: Rule R1 cannot be applied at all. Animal in vivo evidence has nothing to be weighed against, so a clean rodent study carries the whole question by default.

items.field: Bile-salt export pump / hepatobiliary transporter inhibition
items.whatItBlocks: The most common route to cholestatic injury is untested. A cholestatic pattern later seen in humans could not have been anticipated from the package.
items.whyNotApplicable: A monoclonal antibody does not enter hepatocytes or interact with bile-salt export pumps; transporter inhibition is a small-molecule liability.

items.field: Reactive metabolite or covalent binding assessment
items.whatItBlocks: The main route to idiosyncratic injury is unexamined. Idiosyncratic injury is what withdrew most of the drugs this system exists to catch.
items.whyNotApplicable: An antibody is catabolised to amino acids by normal protein turnover. There is no cytochrome-P450 metabolism and therefore no reactive metabolite to trap.

items.whatItBlocks: A key event in the liver-injury pathway is unmeasured, so rule R2 cannot distinguish direct pathway evidence from structural correlation.
items.whyNotApplicable: Mitochondrial toxicity assays measure a small molecule crossing into the mitochondrion. A 150 kDa protein does not get there.

items.whatItBlocks: There is no whole-organism observation, so nothing tests whether an in vitro signal survives absorption, distribution and clearance.

items.field: Structural alert or QSAR assessment, with applicability domain stated
items.whatItBlocks: Rule R4 cannot be applied: a structural prediction with no stated domain cannot be down-weighted for being outside it, so it is either trusted blindly or discarded blindly.
items.whyNotApplicable: QSAR and structural-alert models are trained on small-molecule chemistry. An antibody has no scoreable structure, and a model run outside its applicability domain is exactly what rule R4 exists to exclude.

items.whatItBlocks: Severity cannot be scaled. Dose is the single strongest available predictor of whether a mechanism becomes an injury.

items.field: Exposure margin: tested concentration or NOAEL against projected human Cmax
items.whatItBlocks: Rule R3 cannot be applied to any reassuring result. A clean assay run below the exposure humans will see is not evidence of safety, and without this field the two are indistinguishable.
searchTerms: human exposure at the recommended dose

items.field: Injury pattern: hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed
items.whatItBlocks: The consequence question cannot be answered in kind. Hepatocellular injury and a cholestatic enzyme rise carry different prognoses and different stopping rules.
The difference between a monitorable signal and a programme-stopping one is unstated. Reversible transaminase elevation is managed; irreversible injury is not.

items.field: Expected frequency and the population that would be exposed
items.whatItBlocks: A rate that matters cannot be distinguished from one that does not, and the size of the population that would carry the risk is unknown.
Chronic dosing in an otherwise healthy population and short-course dosing in serious disease tolerate entirely different signals, and nothing distinguishes them.

_whyAppliesTo: Some questions do not arise for some kinds of drug, and reporting them as gaps is the same false alarm as flagging an approved BSEP inhibitor. A monoclonal antibody is catabolised to amino acids, so it has no reactive metabolite; it does not interact with hepatobiliary transporters; and QSAR models are built for small molecules. Those are NOT unanswered questions, they are questions that do not apply, and an inventory that cannot tell the difference teaches people to ignore it. Regulators already make this distinction explicitly - this document's own genotoxicity section reads 'No genotoxicity studies were conducted with nipocalimab. This is considered acceptable.' An item with no appliesTo applies to EVERYTHING: a checklist author who forgets the field gets the question asked rather than silently dropped.
_whyNotApplicableText: Rendered INSTEAD of whatItBlocks when an item does not apply. They answer different questions - whatItBlocks says what goes wrong when a question is unanswered, which is the wrong sentence entirely for a question that does not arise. Showing the gap text beside an n/a badge made four non-issues read as four untested liabilities, which is the false alarm the state was added to prevent.
_searchTermsNote: searchTerms widen the RETRIEVAL query in extract.ts and are never shown to a reader. The field text is written for a person reading a checklist; a regulatory review uses different words for the same fact - 'Projected human daily dose' against 'the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) for ADPKD is 120 mg/day'. Four of the six consequence items returned nothing for that reason on every drug in the corpus, which empties consequenceBasis, which the adjudicator prompt requires to produce cannot_conclude - so every end-to-end verdict was an abstention caused by vocabulary rather than by evidence. Every term here was taken from how the documents actually phrase the dimension. Widening the query cannot create a wrong finding: a proposal still has to carry a verbatim quote and a page and be judged against the field, so a bad passage costs a discarded proposal.
